name: Dibenzylideneacetone

lead: Dibenzylideneacetone is a yellow organic compound whose conjugated structure absorbs light, which is why it is discussed alongside UV-absorbing molecules.
Its established role is as a ligand for palladium in chemical synthesis; laboratory studies of derivatives cover cancer cells, parasites and fungi.

paras: Two phenyl rings linked through a conjugated ketone chain absorb light and bind metals such as palladium.
It is a research chemical with no approved skin or sunscreen use and no human studies on skin protection.

chain: Proposed as a UV-absorbing chemical class
No finished sunscreen product built on it
angle.text: People interested in sunscreen chemistry note that dba is a conjugated, light-absorbing molecule, the same general feature that lets filters shield skin. It is a research chemical, and its use in skin protection is a concept rather than a product.

lead: Dibenzylideneacetone (dba) is a bright-yellow crystalline organic compound with the formula C17H14O, made by condensing acetone with two molecules of benzaldehyde.[1][2] Its two phenyl rings joined through a conjugated chain give it strong light-absorbing character, which is why it is mentioned alongside UV-absorbing, sunscreen-type molecules; Wikipedia lists use as a sunscreen component among its applications.[2]

For skin, the appearance chain is a photoprotection one: a conjugated aromatic ketone that absorbs ultraviolet light could, in a formulation, reduce UV reaching the skin and so help limit sun-driven ageing and pigmentation. This is a concept tied to the molecule's structure rather than a documented consumer routine, and no human study of dba on skin was found.[2]

In practice dba is best known as a laboratory reagent: a ligand for palladium, forming complexes such as tris(dibenzylideneacetone)dipalladium(0), widely used in cross-coupling chemistry.[1][2] Published research on dba and its derivatives covers cancer cell lines, parasites, fungi and imaging agents, all at laboratory stage.[3][4][5][6][7]

paras: The trans,trans isomer is the stable, common form, melting at roughly 110 to 111 C. It is insoluble in water and dissolves in ethanol, acetone and chloroform.[1][2] The molecule has three stereoisomeric forms depending on the geometry of its two double bonds, the (E,E), (E,Z) and (Z,Z) forms, with the cis,trans form melting near 60 C.[2]

It is prepared by a base-catalysed Claisen-Schmidt condensation of benzaldehyde with acetone, usually in a water and ethanol mixture with sodium hydroxide, passing through benzylideneacetone as an intermediate; it is a common teaching experiment.[2] It was first described in 1881 by Rainer Ludwig Claisen and Charles-Claude-Alexandre Claparede.[1][2] Wikipedia notes that prolonged exposure to sunlight causes [2+2] cycloaddition to dimeric and trimeric cyclobutane products.[2]

The dba ligand is labile and easily displaced by triphenylphosphine, so complexes such as tris(dibenzylideneacetone)dipalladium(0) are convenient sources of palladium(0) for synthesis.[2] Crystal structures of palladium-dba complexes have been reported.[8]

Wikipedia states that dba is used as a component in sunscreens, though its principal role is in organometallic chemistry.[2] The same page does not explain the UV absorption mechanism.[2] No study of dba applied to human skin, or of its effect on sunburn or photoageing, was found.

The only hazard listed on Wikipedia is that dba is an irritant.[2] Laboratory research into derivatives involves cytotoxic and antimicrobial activity, which is the reason such compounds are studied in cells and not applied to people.[4][7]

No studies found. Related laboratory research includes: a structure-activity study of 26 dba analogs, developed from the curcumin scaffold, against bloodstream forms of Trypanosoma brucei, with several compounds reaching EC50 values as low as 200 nM and selectivity indices above 10 in HEK293 cells;[3] a synthetic dba derivative that was cytotoxic to HeLa and SiHa cervical cancer cells through reactive oxygen species and mitochondrial damage;[4] dba as an inhibitor of Botrytis cinerea chitinase (IC50 13.1 ug/mL) that extended the shelf life of cherry tomatoes about two-fold;[5] chitosan-dba Schiff bases tested for antimicrobial activity and cytotoxicity;[7] and a tris-dba palladium complex studied in preclinical models of hepatocellular carcinoma and multiple myeloma.[6]

Dba scaffolds have also been explored for 99mTc-labelled imaging agents in Alzheimer's diagnosis.[9] A 2002 pharmacophore study described cross-conjugated dienones, the family to which dba belongs, as inducers of p53-independent cell death.[10]

Dba-based compounds are used as starting points in medicinal chemistry. One report described dba sensitising tumour cells to the TRAIL cytokine through reactive oxygen species and CHOP.[11] These studies do not address use on skin.
